Green coverage metrics included direct indicators such as residential greening [ 28 , 29 , 31 , 42 ], community greening [ 38 , 47 , 48 ], neighborhood landscaping [ 32 ], park cover [ 36 , 37 ], and forest/canopy coverage [ 35 , 54 ]. They also encompassed measures of surrounding green cover derived from NDVI, quantified through remote sensing technology [ 30 , 33 , 34 , 36 , 37 , 39 – 42 , 44 , 45 , 49 , 50 ]. Accessibility indicators emphasized the proximity and availability of green resources such as parks, green spaces, and forests, including the distance to the nearest park and the density of green spaces within a walkable range [ 46 , 52 , 53 ]. At the ecological structure level, the focus was on composite attributes such as the diversity of green space types and the proportion of private gardens [ 37 , 51 ]. Across the included studies, most exposure to green space measurements were based on the participants’ place of residence, with the most common buffer zones ranging from 250 m to 1,000 m. Health outcomes Our findings indicated that the included health outcomes encompassed circulatory system diseases, metabolic diseases, nervous system disorders, cognitive impairments, mental illnesses, and life satisfaction [ 28 – 54 ]. Seven studies examined CVDs. Two of these reported associations between exposure to green space and variations in blood pressure among older adults [ 30 , 54 ]. Another two investigated the effects of exposure to green space on heart health specifically [ 45 , 50 ]. The remaining studies evaluated the association between exposure to green space and CVD from a broader perspective [ 33 , 36 , 40 ]. Three studies focused on metabolic diseases, investigating associations with metabolic disorders in general [ 28 ], dyslipidemia [ 29 ], and diabetes [ 44 ]. Seven studies addressed nervous system diseases. The majority examined the effects of exposure to green space on Alzheimer’s disease (AD) [ 34 , 37 , 41 , 49 ] and cognitive impairment [ 31 , 32 , 35 ]. Two studies also explored the impact of exposure to green space on neurodegenerative diseases more broadly [ 37 , 41 ]. In total, six mental illness studies were included. Four studies focused on geriatric depression [ 38 , 39 , 42 , 43 ], one examined both geriatric depression and geriatric anxiety [ 51 ], and one assessed overall mental health in older adults [ 52 ]. Two studies evaluated the effects of exposure to green space on life satisfaction [ 46 , 53 ]. Additionally, one study analyzed the relationship between exposure to green space and the prevalence of common chronic diseases in older adults [ 48 ], while another simultaneously examined associations with both AD and depression [ 47 ]. Link between green space and health outcomes Green space and circulatory system diseases Seven studies, including four cohort studies, two cross-sectional investigations, and one RCT, examined the relationship between exposure to green space and circulatory diseases such as hypertension, heart disease, and CVD. Together, these studies included 6,349,894 participants, with sample sizes ranging from 24 to 63,009,173 individuals. A meta-analysis was not performed because of substantial variation in the effect size metrics used to report clinical outcomes. Associations between exposure to green space and health outcomes were measured using indicators such as forest and park coverage, as well as mean NDVI values representing surrounding vegetation. Two studies categorized exposure into low, medium, and high levels [ 33 , 50 ], while others calculated NDVI values within buffer zones of 250 m, 500 m, 750 m, and 1,000 m around participants’ homes to determine green space density. Across the seven studies, the findings on the cardiovascular benefits of green space for older adults were not entirely consistent [ 30 , 33 , 36 , 40 , 45 , 50 , 54 ], although a considerable amount of evidence supports a protective effect. In studies on hypertension, one investigation reported a nonlinear, U-shaped association between exposure to green space and the risk of hypertension. The protective effect was especially notable in areas with high green coverage, where each 0.1-unit increase in NDVI was associated with a 40% reduction in hypertension risk [ 30 ]. Another study found that exposure to green space also contributed to the management of hypertension in older adults [ 54 ]. In an RCT, elderly residents exposed to a forest environment experienced significant decreases in diastolic blood pressure, low-frequency heart rate variability, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, as well as significant increases in oxygen saturation and high-frequency heart rate variability [ 55 ]. Two studies showed that high exposure to green space was associated with a reduced risk of CVD [ 33 , 36 ]. Living in greener communities was associated with a 25% lower risk of acute myocardial infarction, a 20 percent lower risk of ischemic heart disease, and a 16% lower risk of heart failure [ 45 , 50 ]. Ruoyu Wang et al. also found that a greater proportion of visible green space in the community was associated with better cardiovascular health in older adults [ 45 ]. Three studies reported no statistically significant association. A cohort study in Spain found no significant link between green space within a 250-m buffer and CVD, although green space within a 500–1,000 m buffer was associated with lower levels of CVD biomarkers, including N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide, high-sensitivity troponin, and interleukin-6 [ 40 ]. In a study of the oldest-old population in China, no significant association was found between low green cover and hypertension risk [ 30 ]. Another Chinese study found no significant relationship between the presence of street trees and cardiovascular health in older adults. Green space and metabolic diseases Three studies, comprising two cohort studies and one cross-sectional study, examined the relationship between exposure to green space and MetS in a total of 88,380 older adults. These studies investigated different health outcomes, including diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and MetS. All three studies used NDVI to quantify exposure to green space, although they differed in the spatial scales applied. One study calculated NDVI within a single 500-m residential buffer zone [ 44 ], while the other two used multiple buffer zones centered on participants’ geocoded residential addresses. Across the three studies, a higher level of exposure to green space was consistently associated with better metabolic health [ 28 , 29 , 44 ]. One study reported that for every 0.1-unit increase in NDVI, the odds of being free from chronic diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia increased by 7% in the overall sample [ 48 ]. Another study found that greater residential greenery was associated with a lower risk of MetS [ 28 ]. Interestingly, one investigation showed that while higher levels of greenery were generally protective, the strength of the association with blood lipid levels diminished as green space increased [ 29 ]. Additionally, overall green coverage was associated with a reduced risk of diabetes, but the proportion of greenery visible in daily life was not significantly associated with diabetes risk [ 44 ]. A meta-analysis was not performed because of differences in outcome measures and effect size reporting across studies. Green space and nervous system diseases Seven studies, including four cohort and three cross-sectional designs, investigated the association between exposure to green space and neurological disorders. The combined sample size across these studies was 1,877,357 participants, with individual sample sizes ranging from 1,125 to 1,134,502. Most studies reported that higher levels of residential greenery were associated with a lower risk of AD or dementia, as well as better cognitive function [ 31 , 32 , 34 , 35 , 37 , 41 , 49 ]. Two cross-sectional studies conducted in the United States found that continuous high exposure to green space was associated with a 16%–20% reduction in AD incidence among older adults [ 34 , 49 ]. Another study examining both AD and depression found that for every 0.1-unit increase in NDVI, the risk of AD decreased by 10% [ 47 ]. A Belgian study reported that for every one interquartile range increase in greenery, total mortality from neurodegenerative diseases decreased by 4%–5% [ 41 ]. Research by Brown et al. showed that younger older adults (age: 65–74 years) living in greener communities had a reduced risk of developing AD and reported better overall health [ 34 ]. The study suggested that these protective effects were mediated through increased physical activity, reduced psychological stress, and stronger social support networks [ 34 ]. Among studies on cognitive impairment, one found that forest coverage was more strongly associated with dementia risk than other green space measures [ 35 ]. The APOEε4 gene, a major genetic risk factor for AD, may reduce the protective effects of green space on cognitive function, as reported in several studies [ 31 , 32 ]. Because of variations in exposure measurements, outcome definitions, and available data, a meta-analysis was conducted for only three studies that reported on AD. The pooled analysis indicated a significant protective effect of exposure to green space on AD in older adults (OR: 0.856, 95% CI: 0.769–0.943), with moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 67.4%, p = 0.046) [ 34 , 35 , 47 ] (Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Forest plot of the effect of green space exposure on Alzheimer's disease Green space and mental illness Six observational studies examined the relationship between exposure to green space and geriatric mental health outcomes in a pooled sample of 284,086 participants, comprising five cross-sectional studies and one cohort study. Five investigations assessed composite mental health indices reflecting overall psychological status, while one study specifically focused on late-life depressive disorders [ 38 , 39 , 42 , 43 , 47 , 52 ]. One study measured both depressive symptoms and anxiety disorders using validated clinical instruments [ 51 ]. Another study on AD and depression found that for every 0.1 increase in NDVI, the risk of depression decreased by 28% [ 47 ]. All included studies reported that exposure to green spaces was associated with a reduced risk of mental illnesses among older adults [ 38 , 39 , 42 , 43 , 47 , 51 , 52 ]. A Norwegian cohort study observed an inverse relationship between residential exposure to green space and psychological distress in older adults, with a stronger dose–response effect in those with better baseline physical health [ 52 ]. In contrast, studies from China found that the association between exposure to green space and depressive symptoms was mediated by physical activity [ 42 , 43 ]. Research from Shanghai and the UK suggested that green communities reduce depression in older adults by fostering social cohesion [ 43 , 51 ]. Another study reported a 15% reduction in depression risk for each 0.1-unit increase in NDVI [ 47 ]. Due to differences in exposure measures and reported outcomes, as well as limited data, a meta-analysis was conducted for only three studies on depression. The pooled results indicated a protective effect of exposure to green space on depression in older adults (OR: 0.724, 95% CI: 0.549–0.900), with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 99.5%, p = 0.000) [ 38 , 47 , 51 ] (Fig. 4 ). A meta-analysis was not conducted due to heterogeneity in effect size metrics. Both studies found that green spaces positively influenced life satisfaction by providing opportunities for outdoor activity, fostering social interaction, and offering aesthetic enjoyment [ 56 ]. Enhanced environmental quality from green spaces was shown to have both direct and indirect effects on residents’ life satisfaction. One study highlighted a positive association between green viewing rate and park accessibility with life satisfaction in older adults [ 46 ]. Another study found that green spaces improved life satisfaction primarily through enhanced environmental quality and a stronger sense of place among residents [ 53 ]. Although we have already described the heterogeneity of each outcome in the results section, some details still need to be elaborated on. These details are provided in Supplementary 1. Discussion This systematic review identified 27 studies that examined the association between exposure to green space and health outcomes among older adults. The number of participants in these studies ranged from 24 to 63,009,173. Notably, only one study did not report gender distribution [ 54 ]. This review systematically analyzed and comprehensively evaluated the impact of exposure to green space on health indicators in older adults. The findings indicated that most evidence consistently supported the beneficial effects of exposure to green space on a range of chronic diseases in this population, with the notable exception of CVD findings. This conclusion regarding the broader range of chronic diseases aligns closely with results from broader population-based studies. However, in the CVD–related studies included in this review, exposure to green space demonstrated a nonlinear, dose–response association with cardiovascular risk in older adults. For instance, a study in Denmark reported no significant correlation between the number of green spaces within 500 m or 1,000 m and CVD risk, but found a protective effect within a 5,000 m radius [ 57 ]. The cardiovascular benefits of high exposure to green space may be attributed to the diversity of green space types, which enhance functionality and expand residents’ daily activity ranges, thereby promoting health. Existing evidence has firmly established the close link between exposure to green space and human health. Critically, while systematic reviews and meta-analyses have firmly established the beneficial links between green space exposure and various health outcomes (including CVD) in broader populations [ 58 , 59 ], the evidence base specific to older adults—a rapidly growing demographic facing unique challenges—remains notably limited. Older adults often face multiple comorbidities. Their pathological, physiological, and psychosocial needs are far more complex than those of younger adults. Despite their high vulnerability and disease burden, there is a current lack of systematic evidence detailing how green space exposure specifically impacts common diseases, including CVD with its observed nonlinear pattern, within this elderly cohort. This review directly addresses this critical gap by synthesizing existing research through systematic review and meta-analysis, focusing on the older adult population and their specific health contexts. Due to differences in exposure measures and outcome metrics across the included studies, we conducted meta-analyses for only two outcomes: depression and cognition. The results revealed a protective effect of exposure to green space on both depression and cognitive function in older adults. Specifically, a 0.1-unit increase in NDVI was associated with a reduced risk of depression [ 60 ]. Other studies have reported that exposure to green space exerts more pronounced mental health benefits in specific age groups (such as 18–24, < 30, and 31–50 years) [ 61 , 62 ]. For example, pregnant women living within 100 m of green space had an 18%–23% lower incidence of depressive symptoms [ 63 ]. Mental health benefits of exposure to green space operate through three primary pathways: physical, psychological, and social. At the cellular level, mitochondria are the “energy factories” of cells, and oxidative stress can impair their function, leading to insufficient neuronal energy supply and triggering apoptosis, which increases depression risk [ 64 , 65 ]. Exposure to green space mitigates these effects by reducing oxidative stress [ 66 ]. Furthermore, higher air pollutant levels are strongly associated with increased risks of depression and anxiety [ 67 – 69 ]. Exposure to green space helps improve mental health by reducing both air and noise pollution. In addition, individuals living in greener areas are more likely to engage in physical activity and participate in social interactions, reducing the likelihood of developing mental health disorders [ 70 , 71 ]. Exposure to green space alleviates depression and anxiety by lowering stress levels, enhancing residents’ sense of well-being, and strengthening social cohesion [ 72 ]. Existing evidence shows a positive correlation between exposure to green space and lifelong markers of AD and related disorders, including overall brain health [ 73 ]. In childhood, high levels of exposure to green space have been strongly associated with better intellectual development, working memory, spatial orientation, and executive function [ 74 , 75 ]. In adulthood and older age, greater exposure is associated with improved cognitive performance across multiple domains and brain regions, along with a lower risk of AD and other dementias [ 76 ]. A recent study found that cognitive scores declined by 0.01 points for every 1% increase in green space coverage [ 77 ]. Green spaces promote cardiovascular health by encouraging physical activity, which in turn helps reduce cognitive decline [ 78 ]. They also improve cognitive outcomes by lowering air pollution levels and trapping particulate matter [ 79 ], while further protecting brain health through stress reduction and increased social engagement [ 80 , 81 ]. The health benefits of exposure to green space among older adults vary according to socioeconomic status, degree of aging, access levels, and environmental conditions. Studies report stronger benefits for those with low socioeconomic status (such as limited income and education) and for younger seniors aged 65–74 years [ 33 , 38 , 41 , 45 ]. This may reflect their greater reliance on local community resources, with green spaces providing essential settings for recreation and social connection [ 38 ]. In physically capable younger seniors, regular use of green spaces for structured outdoor exercise has been associated with better cardiovascular function, improved mental well-being, and greater mobility, underscoring the value of age-targeted urban planning. Some research indicates that the protective effect of green space only becomes apparent beyond a certain exposure threshold. For example, the link between high exposure and reduced hypertension risk is especially clear at higher coverage levels [ 37 ]. Health impacts may also differ depending on the type and diversity of green space. While higher coverage has been associated with lower risks of CVD, dementia, diabetes, and hypertension, larger total green space area alone does not consistently predict better health outcomes [ 49 , 82 ]. Regional variations in green space characteristics and environmental conditions are critical determinants of their associated health benefits. For example, in northern regions, trees undergo seasonal defoliation, and vegetation becomes sparse during winter, which may cause the health-promoting effects of green spaces to be less pronounced during this season [ 45 ]. In the studies included in this review, most measurement standards for assessing the accessibility of green spaces used NDVI to evaluate the level of exposure to green space. The buffer zone range was between 100 and 5,000 m [ 21 ]. Evidence suggests that exposure to green spaces within a smaller buffer zone (100–800 m) is more strongly associated with mental health, whereas exposure within a larger buffer zone (more than 800 m) tends to have a greater impact on physical activity [ 83 , 84 ]. Maas et al. also found that a buffer zone within 1 km shows the strongest correlation with anxiety disorders and depression [ 85 ]. The likely explanation for this finding is that a small buffer zone (100–800 m) corresponds to the distance residents can typically cover within a 10-min walk [ 86 ]. Such proximity is closely tied to daily activities, neighborhood interactions, and community engagement, thereby exerting a direct influence on mental health and social connectedness. Conversely, larger buffer zones (> 800 m) may yield greater environmental health benefits. Extensive green areas have been shown to filter harmful substances, such as particulate matter, from the air while also offering more space for physical activity, which in turn improves a range of health outcomes. This study indicates that exposure to green spaces can improve the overall health of older adults, partly by reducing environmental pollution. It also shows that green spaces exert a mediating influence on the health benefits experienced by older adults. For instance, green spaces can further enhance overall health by improving air quality. Vegetation and green areas can absorb harmful substances such as nitrogen oxides and particulate matter from the atmosphere, thereby improving residents’ overall health status [ 87 , 88 ]. This systematic review also found that older adults’ overall health, social support, and physical activity play pivotal mediating roles in the link between green spaces and health. Research demonstrates that green spaces enhance residents’ sense of well-being and satisfaction, reduce psychological stress, and protect mental health by offering visually appealing surroundings [ 89 ]. Green areas provide open spaces where residents can engage in various forms of physical activity, encouraging more frequent exercise and thus promoting overall well-being [ 90 ]. This conclusion was also supported by our findings. Older adults can enjoy more comfortable walking conditions in areas with higher levels of exposure to green space, which stimulates their willingness to walk and promotes regular physical activity. In public open spaces such as parks and green areas, older adults are also more likely to interact frequently with neighbors, strengthen social bonds, and reduce feelings of loneliness. The process of rapid urbanization has worsened the unequal distribution of public resources, with the issue of equitable green space allocation becoming especially urgent. Historically, the distribution of environmental amenities in cities has been uneven, with privileged residents in affluent neighborhoods enjoying greater access to parks and other green spaces [ 91 ].The theory of environmental justice emphasizes that urban public green space resources should be distributed equitably to ensure that all social groups, especially low-income populations, older adults, and immigrant communities, can equally benefit from the environmental advantages they provide [ 92 , 93 ]. Compared with nonvulnerable groups, vulnerable groups tend to experience greater health gains from access to green spaces [ 94 ]. Our findings further indicate that areas with higher-quality green spaces have better exposure levels for older adults, resulting in more pronounced health benefits. Therefore, in future policy-making processes, it is recommended to revise urban planning standards to expand green areas within the living environments of low-income older adults and to enhance the quality of available green spaces. Furthermore, biodiversity and habitat quality within urban green spaces can influence how people use and engage with these areas [ 95 ]. Higher biodiversity in green spaces has been associated with improved attention restoration, enhanced human well-being, and better mental health outcomes [ 96 , 97 ]. However, in all the studies we reviewed, the evaluation of exposure to green space was limited to three dimensions—availability, accessibility, and visibility. None of the included studies assessed biodiversity. Therefore, we recommend that future research incorporate biodiversity evaluation and systematically examine the health-promoting mechanisms associated with different types of green areas. The present study offers several strengths. First, it is a systematic review specifically examining the effects of green space on older adults. To our knowledge, no comparable study has been conducted. Second, we synthesized the available evidence and proposed a theoretical framework to guide subsequent investigations. Nonetheless, this study has certain limitations. Many of the included studies did not specify the type of vegetation, which prevented a targeted analysis of vegetation-specific health effects and limited the comprehensiveness of the findings. Additionally, inconsistent definitions and measurements of outcome indicators across studies meant that fewer indicators could be included in the meta-analysis. The substantial heterogeneity observed in the two pooled indicators was primarily attributable to variations in measurement tools and differences in population characteristics. Conclusions This research synthesized the multidimensional health impacts of green environments on aging populations through a systematic review and critical appraisal of empirical studies examining exposure to green space and health outcomes in older adults. The evidence-based framework identifies strong associations between green space accessibility and quality with geriatric health indicators, providing a solid empirical basis for developing nature-based behavioral interventions. These findings present actionable guidance for a wide range of stakeholders, particularly urban planners and public health policymakers, to integrate green infrastructure design into strategies for creating age-friendly, health-enhancing communities. documents.title: Efficacy and safety of curved vertebroplasty in osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Curved vertebroplasty (CVP), including percutaneous curved vertebroplasty (PCVP) and percutaneous curved kyphoplasty (PCKP), represents a novel surgical modality in recent years for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures (OVCFs). Although numerous clinical studies have reported its safety and efficacy, meta-analyses remain necessary to further validate the robustness of this evidence. METHODS: Based on the PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive literature search of four databases—PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science—for all relevant studies published from their inception to April 2025. Two investigators independently conducted a quality assessment, extracted the data, and performed all statistical analyses. In case of disagreement, a third investigator adjudicated the risk of bias assessment. RESULTS: A total of nine studies involving 814 patients with OVCFs were included, comprising five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and four retrospective cohort studies (RCS). Among these, two RCTs and all RCS investigated PCVP, while the remaining three RCTs evaluated PCKP. The meta-analysis showed that compared with Percutaneous vertebral augmentation (PVA), CVP had comparable effects in terms of visual analog scale (VAS), Oswestry disability index (ODI), and improvement of the COBB angle, but significantly improved the surgical efficiency. Subgroup analysis revealed that PCVP and PCKP could consistently reduce the operation time (MD = -9.59, 95% CI: -18.93, -0.24; MD = -14.00, 95% CI: -22.40, -5.60) and the number of intraoperative fluoroscopy (MD = -5.89, 95% CI: -9.48, -2.29; MD = -26.32, 95% CI: -45.95, -6.68). However, PCVP could reduce the risk of bone cement leakage and the volume of bone cement (OR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.24, 0.70; MD = -1.40, 95% CI: -2.29, 0.51). CONCLUSIONS: CVP is a feasible option for treating patients with OVCFs, which could effectively enhance surgical efficiency without reducing clinical efficacy. However, its effectiveness and long-term advantages in a broader population still need to be further verified.

Introduction As the global population continues to age, OVCFs are one of the major health problems worldwide [ 1 ]. OVCFs are known to cause substantial pain and deformity, which in turn leads to disability and significantly increased the risk of adjacent vertebrae fractures [ 2 ]. Although the treatment of anti-osteoporosis drugs can reduce the incidence of OVCFs, there is still a large number of OVCFs [ 3 , 4 ]. Meanwhile, patients with OVCFs are not satisfied with conservative treatment [ 5 , 6 ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need in clinical practice for treatment methods that can rapidly and effectively alleviate symptoms and restore spinal stability. PVA, a well-established minimally invasive intervention for OVCFs, is widely utilized due to its favorable clinical outcomes and therapeutic potential [ 7 , 8 ]. This technique stabilizes fractured vertebrae through cement injection, enhancing vertebral structural integrity to prevent collapse and alleviate pain with documented efficacy [ 9 ]. Current clinical practice primarily employs two PVA modalities: percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) and percutaneous kyphoplasty (PKP). However, the traditional PVA technique has certain limitations, especially in achieving the symmetrical distribution of bone cement within the vertebrae through the unilateral pedicle approach [ 10 ]. This may affect the uniformity of load transmission and the long-term durability of the therapeutic effect [ 11 ]. With the continuous advancement of minimally invasive spinal techniques, CVP, as an evolved technology from traditional PVA, has been introduced, including PCKP and PCVP [ 12 , 13 ]. This improved method employs a specially designed curved delivery system, allowing the puncture needle to turn within the vertebra, thereby enabling the bone cement to be targetedly infused into the contralateral half of the vertebral body without the need for an extreme pedicle trajectory [ 14 ]. By promoting more controllable and symmetrical bone cement dispersion, CVP aims to enhance the biomechanical reinforcement effect, improve clinical outcomes, and potentially reduce surgical-related complications such as bone cement leakage, paravertebral vein embolism, and radiation exposure due to repeated fluoroscopic adjustments [ 15 ]. Although preliminary studies report high satisfaction rates with CVP for OVCFs management [ 12 , 16 ]. However, reliable and direct comparative evidence assessing its therapeutic efficacy and safety compared to traditional PVA remains limited and sometimes inconsistent. In particular, whether the theoretical advantages of curved instruments can translate into clinically significant benefits has not been clearly concluded through the systematic synthesis of existing evidence. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis quantitatively compares CVP and PVA from multiple perioperative and clinical outcome perspectives, aiming to draw evidence-based conclusions regarding their relative safety and efficacy for patients with OVCFs. Materials and methods Protocol, registration and search strategy Literature searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from inception through April 2025. Search strategies incorporated MeSH terms (“Osteoporotic Fractures,” “Curved Vertebroplasty,” “PVP,” “PKP”) and relevant keywords, structured according to PICOS criteria [ 17 , 18 ]. Two independent investigators performed study selection using predefined eligibility criteria, resolving discrepancies through consensus. In case of disagreement, a third investigator adjudicated the risk of bias assessment. This study complied with Preferred reporting items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses [ 17 ] (PRISMA) and assessing methodological quality of systematic reviews [ 18 ] (AMSTAR) guidelines. A detailed PRISMA and AMSTAR checklist is provided in Supplementary Material. The manuscript is compliant with the TITAN Guidelines 2025 – governing the declaration and use of artificial intelligence (AI) [ 19 ]. Selection criteria Inclusion criteria were defined per PICOS framework: (1). Population: Adults with radiologically confirmed OVCFs. (2). Intervention: CVP or its derivatives PCVP/PCKP. (3). Comparator: PVA, including PVP or PKP. (4). Outcomes: ≥ 1 outcome metric from: Patient-reported outcomes: Oswestry disability index (ODI) or VAS, Radiographic parameters: Cobb angle or number of X-ray fluoroscopy, Safety endpoints: Bone cement leakage rate, Resource utilization: Bone cement injection volume (mL), operative time (minutes). (5). Study design: RCT or RCS. Exclusion criteria: (1). Single-arm investigations without comparative data. (2). Non-original research (reviews, ase reports, editorials). (3). Non-human studies (cadaveric/animal models). (4). Publications with incomplete or non-extractable outcome data. For duplicate publications, the most comprehensive dataset was prioritized per PRISMA duplication guidelines [ 17 , 18 ]. Data extraction Data extraction was performed independently by two investigators using a predesigned standardized form. The following domains were systematically extracted:Study attributes: First author and publication year. Participant characteristics: Diagnosis, sex, mean age, and follow-up duration. Interventional parameters: Surgical technique (CVP/PVA) and vertebral level treated. Efficacy outcomes: Patient-reported pain and function: VAS and ODI. Radiographic assessment: Cobb angle or number of X-ray fluoroscopy. Complications: Cement leakage incidence. Procedural metrics: Cement injection volume (mL) and Operative time (minutes). Quality of the evidence Records retrieved from all databases were deduplicated using EndNote. Two independent reviewers conducted a two-stage screening process: initial exclusion based on titles/abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible studies. Discrepancies in extracted data were resolved through iterative discussion until consensus was achieved, with adjudication by a senior investigator when necessary. Risk of bias was assessed according to the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) for RCS [ 20 ] and the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for RCT [ 21 , 22 ]. Statistical analysis All meta-analyses were conducted by Review manager 5.4 and stata 14.0. For the continuous outcomes such as the ODI and VAS, the mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were used for estimates. For dichotomous outcomes such as the rate of complications, odds ratio (OR) and 95% CI were calculated. Statistical significance was identified by P values < 0.05. The level of statistical heterogeneity was assessed by the I-square test. I-square values of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicated low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. When I-square < 50%, a fixed-effect model was applied, and when I-square > 50%, a random-effect model was applied. If significant heterogeneity existed, subgroup analysis was used to find the source of heterogeneity. Treatment effects in subgroups were compared by a test of interaction (using Cochran’s Q test and I-square) [ 23 ]. To assess the robustness of the meta-analysis findings, we performed sensitivity analyses using the leave-one-out method for all primary outcomes. All quantitative analysis results were demonstrated using forest plots. The potential publication bias was not assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s test because the number of studies included in each analysis was < 10, in which case the funnel plots and Egger’s test could yield misleading results [ 22 ]. Based on the PRISMA reporting guidelines [ 17 ], when meta-analysis results from RCT and RCS demonstrate conflict, the primary conclusions should prioritize evidence derived from RCT. Results Included studies A total of 2341 papers were preliminarily retrieved from searches of the various electronic databases. First, 850 articles remained after the duplicates were removed with Endnote software. Then, we read the titles and abstracts and rejected 818 irrelevant studies. Based on the eligibility and exclusion criteria, 22 studies were excluded. According to the NOS, 1 low-quality study was excluded. Finally, 9 eligible articles were included in this meta-analysis [ 12 – 16 , 24 – 27 ]. The flow chart of the literature search process is shown in Fig. 1 and Table 1 . The intervention was PCVP with five studies [ 13 – 15 , 24 , 26 , 27 ], and the remaining studies were PCKP [ 12 , 16 , 25 ]. The basic characteristics of the patients in the included studies, such as age and sex, were comparable. The quality assessment of RCT and RCS studies is provided in the Supplementary Material. Meta-analysis Clinical outcomes All studies [ 12 – 16 , 24 – 27 ] presented VAS data. The meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCVP and PVP in the preoperation (MD = −0.08, 95% CI −0.24, 0.07, P = 0.30), postoperation 24 h (MD = −0.30, 95 CI% −0.70, 0.10, P = 0.14), three months after surgery (MD = −0.11, 95 CI% −0.25, 0.03, P = 0.12) and six months after surgery (MD = −0.16, 95 CI% −0.37, 0.06, P = 0.15). However, at the one year after surgery, the VAS of PCVP was lower than PVP, which was statistically significant (MD = −0.15, 95% CI −0.28, −0.01, P = 0.04). The meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCKP and PKP in the preoperation (MD = 0.47, 95% CI −0.15, 1.09, P = 0.14), postoperation 24 h (MD = −0.05, 95 CI% −0.23, 0.13, P = 0.60), six months after surgery (MD = 0.06, 95 CI% −0.08, 0.20, P = 0.39) and one year after surgery (MD = −0.07, 95% CI −0.22, 0.09, P = 0.40). Statistical results of subgroup analyses and forest plots are provided in the Supplementary Material. 8 studies [ 12 , 13 , 15 , 16 , 24 – 27 ] provided ODI data. Similarly, the meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCVP and PVP in the preoperation (MD = 0.85, 95% CI −0.35, 2.06, P = 0.17), postoperation 24 h (MD = −2.21, 95 CI% −7.74, 3.32, P = 0.43), three months after surgery (MD = −1.77, 95 CI% −3.68, 0.14, P = 0.07), six months after surgery (MD = −0.22, 95 CI% −1.66, 1.62, P = 0.98) and one year after surgery (MD = −0.15, 95 CI% −1.74, 1.45, P = 0.86). The meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCKP and PKP in the preoperation (MD = −0.77, 95% CI −2.72, 1.18, P = 0.44), postoperation 24 h (MD = −0.20, 95 CI% −1.82, 1.42, P = 0.81), six months after surgery (MD = 0.26, 95 CI% −1.31, 1.82, P = 0.75) and one year after surgery (MD = 6.90, 95 CI% −1.83, 15.63, P = 0.12). Statistical results of subgroup analyses and forest plots are provided in the Supplementary Material. Radiographic outcome Five studies [ 12 , 13 , 15 , 16 , 25 ] reported the cobb angle. However, when comparing the situations of PCVP and PVP, only two studies reported the data on Cobb angles (one RCT and one RCS). [ 13 , 15 ]. We did not conduct a quantitative meta-analysis for this subgroup. Both studies indicated that in terms of the improvement of the Cobb angle after surgery, PCVP showed a statistically more significant improvement compared to PVP. The meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCKP and PKP in the preoperation (MD = 0.00, 95% CI −1.80, 1.81, P = 1.00), postoperation 24 h (MD = −0.45, 95 CI% −1.81, 0.91, P = 0.51), six months after surgery (MD = −0.30, 95 CI% −1.68, 1.07, P = 0.67) and one year after surgery (MD = −0.17, 95 CI% −1.74, 1.40, P = 0.83). Statistical results of subgroup analyses and forest plots are provided in the Supplementary Material. 8 studies [ 12 – 14 , 16 , 24 – 27 ] reported the number of X-ray fluoroscopy. In the meta-analysis of PCVP and PVP, the RCT subgroup analysis showed that the number of X-ray fluoroscopy during PCVP was significantly reduced (MD = −9.69, 95 CI% −10.51, −8.87, P = 0.00, Fig. 2 A). In contrast, in the RCS subgroup, no significant difference was observed between the two groups (MD = −3.41, 95 CI% −7.12, 0.30, P = 0.07, Fig. 2 A). P = 0.001 for the test of difference between subgroups, suggesting that study design may be the main source of heterogeneity. According to the PRISMA reporting guidelines [ 17 ], evidence from RCT is given priority as the main conclusion. In the meta-analysis of PCKP and PKP, the number of the number of X-ray fluoroscopy during PCKP was significantly reduced (MD = −26.32, 95% CI% −45.95, −6.68, P = 0.00, Fig. 2 B). Fig. 2 Forest plot of the number of X-ray fluoroscopy. A : PCVP and PVP. B : PCKP and PKP Perioperative complications Eight studies [ 12 – 15 , 24 – 27 ] presented bone cement leakage rate. In the meta-analysis of PCVP and PVP, the bone cement leakage rate was significantly lower in PCVP compared to the PVP (OR = 0.41, 95% CI 0.24, 0.70, P = 0.00, Fig. 3 A). However, the meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCKP and PKP in the bone cement leakage rate(OR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.24, 1.17, P = 0.12, Fig. 3 B). Fig. 3 Forest plot of bone cement leakage rate. A : PCVP and PVP. B : PCKP and PKP Intraoperative resource consumption All studies [ 12 – 16 , 24 – 27 ] reported information about bone cement volume. In the meta-analysis of PCVP and PVP, the bone cement volume was significantly lower in PCVP compared to the PVP (MD = −1.40, 95% CI −2.29, −0.51, P = 0.00, Fig. 4 A). The meta-analysisi showed that no differences between PCKP and PKP in the bone cement volume (MD = −0.51, 95% CI −1.03, 0.02, P = 0.06, Fig. 4 B). Fig. 4 Forest plot of bone cement volume. A : PCVP and PVP. B : PCKP and PKP All studies [ 12 – 16 , 24 – 27 ] presented operative time. In the meta-analysis of PCVP and PVP, the RCT subgroup analysis showed that operation time during PCVP was significantly reduced (MD = −18.23, 95 CI% −21.63, −14.84, P = 0.00, Fig. 5 A). In contrast, in the RCS subgroup, no significant difference was observed between the two groups (MD = −5.42, 95 CI% −12.87, 2.04, P = 0.15, Fig. 5 A). P = 0.002 for the test of difference between subgroups, suggesting that study design may be the main source of heterogeneity. According to the PRISMA reporting guidelines [ 17 ], evidence from RCT is given priority as the main conclusion. In the meta-analysis of PCKP and PKP, the operation time during PCKP was significantly reduced (MD = −14.00, 95% CI% −22.40, −5.60, P = 0.00, Fig. 5 B). Fig. 5 Forest plot of operative time. A : PCVP and PVP. B : PCKP and PKP Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analysis was conducted using the leave-one-out method. Sequential exclusion of individual studies demonstrated methodological robustness, as the pooled effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals remained within prespecified equivalence margins without directional reversal. This confirms minimal influence of any single study on the meta-analytic conclusions. Comprehensive sensitivity assessments for main outcomes—including fluoroscopy frequency, cement leakage rate, cement volumes, and operative duration—are detailed in Supplementary Material. Discussion In recent years, PVA has gained widespread acceptance as an effective treatment for OVCFs [ 28 ]. With advances in minimally invasive spinal surgery, CVP has emerged as a promising modification aimed at improving clinical outcomes and reducing complications. Although there have been related reports [ 12 , 15 , 16 ] on the safety and efficacy of CVP, due to the lack of comprehensive studies comparing the clinical outcomes of both surgical procedures, the efficacy and safety of CVP for OVCFs remains controversial. So, the purpose of this meta-analysis is to systematically compare surgical approaches (CVP and PVA) for the treatment of OVCFs. Regarding clinical outcomes, this meta-analysis found comparable efficacy for PCVP vs. PVP and PCKP vs. PKP at most follow-up intervals.However, at the one year after surgery, the VAS of PCVP was lower than PVP, which was statistically significant. According to the existing literature, the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of the pain VAS is usually between 0.5 and 4.6 points [ 29 ]. Therefore, this minor difference does not have clinical significance and should not be interpreted as evidence that PCVP has clinical superiority. Bone cement leakage is the most important complication of PVA. Huang et al. [ 30 ] showed that fracture-related parameters and high-dose bone cement injection are independent risk factors for bone cement leakage. Indeed, cortical fractures are the most likely to leak [ 31 ]. Meanwhile, different surgical procedures may also be a factor that affects bone cement leakage, especially PVP [ 32 ], mainly because it involves a high-pressure injection. In addition, the bone cement will spread along the paths offering the least resistance to the vertebral body and fracture [ 33 ]. In CVP, the curved injection device can easily access the contralateral hemivertebrae body. The curved injection device was withdrawn point-by-point, and bone cement was injected at each point [ 15 , 27 ]. Compared with a single high-pressure delivery, low-pressure delivery at multiple points allows for adequate distribution of the cement, while also minimizing the risk of intra-spinal or intravenous leakage [ 34 ]. Generally, bone cement volumes used clinically are 2–3 mL for thoracic and 3–5 mL for lumbar vertebrae [ 35 ]. According to a study by Fu et al. [ 36 ], there was a positive dose–response correlation between bone cement volume with the bone cement leakage after PVP. A clinical study on the relationship between the volumetric analysis of bone cement in vertebroplasty with clinical outcome and complications showed that a volume larger than 11.65% led to a significantly increased incidence of bone cement leakage [ 37 ]. This is supported by previous studies [ 30 , 38 ]. Based on the findings of this meta-analysis, PCVP could reduce the risk of bone cement leakage and volume of bone cement. From a technical principle perspective, the angulation system enables targeted bone cement infusion to the contralateral half of the vertebral body through a unilateral pedicle approach [ 13 ]. This theoretically reduces the number of punctures and damage to the puncture path, which may be related to a lower risk of leakage [ 12 ]. However, there is currently a lack of biomechanical studies directly comparing the pressure dynamics within the vertebral body of the angulation system with that of the straight needle system. Meanwhile, most of the included studies did not report detailed morphological characteristics of fractures (such as AO Spine classification, cortical integrity, and posterior wall involvement). Due to the lack of these stratification information, the combined analysis of the bone cement leakage rate and volume of bone cement in this review cannot conduct a refined assessment of different fracture types, significantly weakening the interpretative ability for the mechanism of safety outcomes. Therefore, the conclusion that the angulation technique reduces the risk of leakage should be regarded as a preliminary trend. Its safety in high-risk fractures (such as burst fractures, posterior wall involved fractures) still needs further verification. Prolonged operative duration increases perioperative risks for medically compromised patients through elevated anesthetic requirements and imposes greater economic burdens [ 39 , 40 ]. Concurrently, excessive radiation exposure during PVA procedures poses significant occupational hazards to surgical teams, with a 0.004% cancer risk increase per 1 mSv dose—substantially higher than other orthopedic interventions [ 39 , 41 ]. Our meta-analysis revealed that PCVP and PCKP could consistently reduce the operation time and the number of intraoperative fluoroscopy. More specifically, CVP did not adjust the puncture angle frequently because of the angle of introversion [ 15 , 27 ]. It is particularly important to note that the statistical advantages of efficiency indicators such as operation time and the number of fluoroscopy sessions mainly stem from RCT evidence. These advantages have not been consistently confirmed in observational studies in the real world. The efficiency advantage of the curved angle technique may only be fully realized with specific operator experience and patient selection conditions. Clinicians should consider their own learning curve and patient composition when introducing this technique and carefully evaluate the expected benefits. In this review, multiple key indicators exhibit extreme heterogeneity (I 2 > 80%), which significantly limits our confidence in the interpretation of the combined effect size and the general applicability of the conclusions. Although we conducted subgroup analyses based on study design and surgical type, the heterogeneity still could not be completely eliminated, suggesting the presence of other uncontrolled clinical confounding factors, including operator experience, differences in instrument design, morphological characteristics of fractures, and differences in vertebral segments, etc. Sensitivity analysis failed to identify a single source of heterogeneity, further confirming the multiplicity of heterogeneity. Therefore, the combined results of these highly heterogeneous indicators should be regarded as exploratory evidence rather than definitive conclusions. In summary, compared with traditional straight-needle techniques, PCVP demonstrates statistical advantages in operation time, fluoroscopy frequency, cement volume, and leakage risk, while PCKP shows benefits in operation time and fluoroscopy frequency. For core clinical outcomes including pain relief and functional recovery, curved techniques are largely equivalent to conventional approaches. However, these findings must be interpreted within the context of important limitations: all included studies were conducted at single centers in China, limiting external validity; variations in curved instrument designs across studies may introduce bias; and substantial heterogeneity in key surgical parameters reduces confidence in pooled estimates. Accordingly, curved vertebroplasty techniques represent feasible options for improving surgical efficiency, but their effectiveness across diverse populations and healthcare settings, as well as potential differences among instrument designs, require validation through international, multicenter studies with standardized protocols. Based on the findings of this systematic review, the following recommendations for clinical practice are proposed: For patients undergoing vertebroplasty, PCVP may be prioritized over conventional PVP. It provides comparable clinical efficacy in terms of pain relief and functional recovery, while offering significant advantages in operative efficiency—including reduced operative time, fewer fluoroscopic exposures, lower cement volume, and decreased leakage risk. These benefits may enhance procedural safety and reduce radiation exposure for both patients and surgical staff. In cases requiring kyphoplasty, PCKP demonstrates superior operative time and fluoroscopy outcomes compared to PKP. However, given the limited evidence base, its broader adoption warrants caution. PCKP may be considered a viable alternative when balloon-assisted reduction is clinically indicated, such as in patients with marked kyphotic deformity. The efficiency gains associated with curved techniques are likely influenced by surgeon experience. Adequate training and awareness of the learning curve are recommended, particularly during initial adoption. The potential of curved techniques to reduce cement leakage may be especially relevant in fractures with cortical disruption or posterior wall involvement. However, this hypothesis requires confirmation through dedicated comparative studies. The advantage of reduced fluoroscopy exposure is particularly meaningful in obese patients, complex fractures, or multilevel procedures where cumulative radiation dose is a concern. In summary, curved vertebroplasty techniques represent an evolution in minimally invasive spinal surgery that improves procedural efficiency without compromising patient-centered outcomes. Clinical adoption should be guided by individual patient characteristics, surgeon expertise, and institutional resources. Limitation One of the main limitations of this review lies in the heterogeneity of the research designs. Although we conducted subgroup analyses based on the research designs, the inherent selection bias and confounding factors in retrospective studies may still affect the reliability of the results. Moreover, all the included studies were from a single center in China, which limits the external validity of the conclusions. Therefore, for the inconsistent findings between RCT and RCS results, we consider them as exploratory conclusions and require further multi-center RCT verification. Conclusions The meta-analysis showed that compared with PVA, CVP had comparable effects in terms of VAS, ODI, and improvement of the COBB angle, but significantly improved the surgical efficiency. PCVP outperforms PVP in terms of reducing the operation time, the number of X-ray fluoroscopy sessions, the volume of bone cement and the risk of leakage. PCKP is superior to PKP in shortening the operation time and reducing the number of X-ray fluoroscopy sessions. The current evidence indicates that CVP is a feasible option that can effectively improve surgical efficiency without compromising clinical efficacy. However, its effect and long-term advantages in a broader population still need to be verified by more high-quality, multi-center international studies. documents.title: Hypercalcemia after denosumab discontinuation in patients with osteoporosis: a systematic review and case report.
documents.abstract:
Discontinuation of denosumab may result in rebound bone resorption, fractures, and rarely hypercalcemia, a very uncommon manifestation. Our systematic review and case report highlight that although rare, calcium disturbances occur after treatment withdrawal. These findings emphasize the importance of sequential antiresorptive therapy and close monitoring in osteoporosis patients.
BACKGROUND: Denosumab discontinuation has been associated with rebound bone resorption, rapid bone loss, and vertebral fractures. Hypercalcemia remains exceptional in postmenopausal osteoporosis.
METHODS: We conducted a PRISMA-based systematic review up to April 2025, including case reports and series describing hypercalcemia after denosumab withdrawal in osteoporosis. We report one additional case.
RESULTS: Three studies (encompassing four women, aged 64-86 years) met the inclusion criteria. All had received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 3-10 years, without prior bisphosphonate exposure. Hypercalcemia (range, 11.3-13.0 mg/dL), developed 3-11 months after discontinuation, was mild to moderate, and asymptomatic. Bone turnover markers were markedly elevated, with low or suppressed intact parathyroid hormone levels. Two patients sustained multiple vertebral fractures. Management consisted of reinitiation of bisphosphonates or denosumab.
CONCLUSIONS: Hypercalcemia after denosumab withdrawal in osteoporosis is rare, typically mild, and reflects rebound osteoclast activation. Sequential antiresorptive therapy is strongly recommended following denosumab discontinuation.

Abstract Summary Discontinuation of denosumab may result in rebound bone resorption, fractures, and rarely hypercalcemia, a very uncommon manifestation. Our systematic review and case report highlight that although rare, calcium disturbances occur after treatment withdrawal. These findings emphasize the importance of sequential antiresorptive therapy and close monitoring in osteoporosis patients. Background Denosumab discontinuation has been associated with rebound bone resorption, rapid bone loss, and vertebral fractures. Hypercalcemia remains exceptional in postmenopausal osteoporosis. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-based systematic review up to April 2025, including case reports and series describing hypercalcemia after denosumab withdrawal in osteoporosis. We report one additional case. Results Three studies (encompassing four women, aged 64–86 years) met the inclusion criteria. All had received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 3–10 years, without prior bisphosphonate exposure. Hypercalcemia (range, 11.3–13.0 mg/dL), developed 3–11 months after discontinuation, was mild to moderate, and asymptomatic. Bone turnover markers were markedly elevated, with low or suppressed intact parathyroid hormone levels. Two patients sustained multiple vertebral fractures. Management consisted of reinitiation of bisphosphonates or denosumab. Conclusions Hypercalcemia after denosumab withdrawal in osteoporosis is rare, typically mild, and reflects rebound osteoclast activation. Sequential antiresorptive therapy is strongly recommended following denosumab discontinuation. Introduction Osteoporosis is the most prevalent metabolic bone disorder, characterized by structural deterioration and reduced bone mass, leading to an increased risk of fragility fractures. It mainly affects postmenopausal women and men over the age of 50. The underlying pathophysiological mechanism involves an imbalance in bone remodeling, characterized by a relative increase in osteoclastic resorption compared to osteoblast-mediated bone formation [ 1 ]. Therapeutic strategies can be broadly classified according to their molecular targets and metabolic effects into osteoanabolic and antiresorptive agents. Among the latter, aminobisphosphonates and denosumab are the most commonly used antiosteoporotic agents. Denosumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds to and inhibits RANK ligand (RANKL), thereby suppressing osteoclast proliferation, function, and survival. By inhibiting RANKL signaling, denosumab effectively reduces bone resorption, attenuates bone mineral density (BMD) loss, and lowers the risk of fracture, establishing its role as a standard treatment for osteoporosis [ 2 ]. Beyond osteoporosis, denosumab has demonstrated efficacy in other skeletal disorders such as Paget’s disease, hypercalcemia of malignancy, primary hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma, bone metastases, and osteogenesis imperfecta [ 2 – 4 ]. It is well established that abrupt discontinuation of denosumab in patients with osteoporosis may trigger a “rebound” phenomenon, characterized by accelerated bone resorption and rapid BMD loss. This is reflected in a marked increase in biochemical bone turnover markers and a significant decrease in BMD, which have been related to the development of multiple vertebral fractures [ 4 – 7 ]. Some cases of hypercalcemia following abrupt denosumab withdrawal have been reported. Such cases predominantly occur in patients with underlying hyperparathyroidism or in children treated for rare skeletal disorders (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta, fibrous dysplasia) [ 7 – 10 ]. This study aims to review, according to PRISMA guidelines, the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of patients with postmenopausal osteoporosis who developed hypercalcemia after denosumab discontinuation, including an additional case from our institution. Patients and methods Eligibility criteria This review followed the PRISMA (“Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses”) recommendations [ 11 ]. We included single case reports and case series in English or Spanish that described hypercalcemia after denosumab withdrawal in patients treated for osteoporosis. Information sources and search strategy A systematic search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science up to April 30, 2025, without restrictions on start date. Additionally, the reference lists of included studies were screened for further relevant publications. The search strategy combined MeSH terms and keywords such as “denosumab,” “hypercalcemia,” “osteoporosis,” “withdrawal,” and “treatment discontinuation.” Full search codes are provided in the Supplementary Material. Inclusion and exclusion criteria We included clinical case reports, case series, and systematic reviews describing patients with osteoporosis who developed hypercalcemia after denosumab discontinuation, and provided full-text availability. Denosumab discontinuation was defined as failure to receive the scheduled 60 mg dose at 6 months. This definition was applied uniformly across all included studies. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (a) hypercalcemia unrelated to denosumab withdrawal, (b) indication for denosumab other than osteoporosis, or (c) use of other antiresorptive agents instead of denosumab. Study selection One reviewer initially screened all titles and abstracts, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were subsequently assessed. The selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram for study inclusion Data extraction From each study, we extracted the following data (see Table 1 ): baseline BMD before denosumab therapy; prior fracture history; treatment duration and dosing; post-withdrawal biochemical parameters (serum calcium, intact PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, bone turnover markers); occurrence of new fractures; time to hypercalcemia onset after last denosumab dose; and prescribed therapy. After removing duplicates, 25 articles remained for full evaluation. Of these, 21 were excluded based on title, abstract, or full-text screening, and one was excluded due to publication in a language other than English or Spanish. Finally, three studies were included for qualitative synthesis. The study selection process is illustrated in Fig. 1 using the PRISMA flow diagram. Characteristics of the included studies Two studies reported individual case reports, while Camponovo et al. presented a systematic review of hypercalcemia for any indication, which included three osteoporosis cases (one newly reported). The studies were carried out in France, Switzerland, and Denmark, and were published between 2016 and 2020. Findings of individual studies We analyzed four clinical cases of postmenopausal women aged 64–86 (median 76.5) years who had received standard-dose denosumab (60 mg every 6 months) for 3–10 years. None of them had prior exposure to other antiresorptive drugs. All cases met the criteria for severe osteoporosis. Three (75%) had sustained fragility fractures before denosumab onset, predominantly vertebral, humeral, or distal radius. Baseline lumbar spine T-scores were ≤ −2.5 in all patients. Following denosumab discontinuation, all patients developed hypercalcemia within 3–11 months (median 6.5). Total serum calcium ranged from 11.3 to 13.03 mg/dL. Hypercalcemia was mild to moderate and clinically asymptomatic in all the patients. Bone turnover markers were markedly elevated, with a median serum C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX) levels of 1.74 ng/mL (normal range for postmenopausal women: 0.10–0.60 ng/mL). Intact parathormone (PTH) concentrations were suppressed (< 20 pg/mL) in three patients and within the reference range in one. With regard to 25-OH vitamin D concentrations, two patients had low levels (< 20 ng/mL), one patient had values within the normal range (20–60 ng/mL), and one patient had increased serum vitamin D levels (77 ng/mL). Two patients (50%) developed multiple vertebral fractures after denosumab withdrawal. Management included bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or alendronate) in three patients, while denosumab was reinitiated in one. Discussion In this study, we systematically reviewed the available literature on hypercalcemia following denosumab discontinuation in osteoporosis, and an additional case is reported. Using PRISMA methodology, we included reports since the drug’s first pivotal trials and subsequent approval in 2010. Denosumab discontinuation has consistently been associated with rebound bone resorption. In the DATA trial, patients switching from denosumab to teriparatide had marked increases in serum CTX levels and marked decreases in BMD, attributed to reactivation of osteoclasts via the RANKL pathway. Nevertheless, this effect has not been observed with bisphosphonates [ 12 ]. The increase in resorption that occurs after denosumab withdrawal has been associated with an increase in the number of fractures. Temporary factors, such as the COVID-19 pandemic have also highlighted the clinical impact of treatment adherence, since missed or delayed denosumab injections were shown to compromise continuity of therapy [ 13 ]. In the FREEDOM trial, up to 7% of patients experienced fractures following denosumab discontinuation [ 14 ]. However, the largest study to date, a post hoc analysis of FREEDOM and its extension, including 1471 patients, showed that the overall incidence of new fractures was not higher in the denosumab discontinuation group compared with placebo (vertebral fractures: 7.1 vs. 8.5 per 100 patient-years; non-vertebral fractures: 2.8 vs. 3.8 per 100 patient-years, respectively). Importantly, patients who sustained vertebral fractures after denosumab withdrawal exhibited a markedly higher proportion of multiple vertebral fractures compared with placebo (60.7% vs. 38.7%), underscoring the clinical relevance and severity of these events in this subgroup. In most cases, these fractures occur between 2 and 10 months after denosumab discontinuation, with the strongest predictor being a prior vertebral fracture, either before or during treatment. These findings suggest that while the absolute fracture risk may not differ substantially, the pattern and multiplicity of vertebral fractures post-discontinuation warrant careful monitoring and consideration of sequential antiresorptive strategies [ 12 ]. Thus, according to the position statement of the European Calcified Tissue Society (ECTS), discontinuation of denosumab is associated with an increased risk of multiple, often simultaneous, vertebral fractures, predominantly affecting the thoracic and lumbar spine. The main risk factors identified include a prior history of vertebral fractures, prolonged exposure to denosumab, lack of subsequent sequential antiresorptive therapy, and low residual BMD [ 5 ]. Regarding calcium metabolism, hypocalcemia during denosumab treatment is generally uncommon, as observed in the FREEDOM study [ 14 ], but its risk is significantly higher in patients with severe chronic kidney disease, malabsorption syndromes, or hypoparathyroidism. In these high-risk populations, the incidence can reach 14–15%, typically peaking around 10 days after administration [ 16 ]. However, hypercalcemia after denosumab withdrawal is less well recognized. Horiuchi et al . found that this complication occurred predominantly in patients with hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, or pediatric bone diseases [ 17 ]. Our review focused exclusively on patients with osteoporosis, in which we identified only three previously reported cases in addition to our own, highlighting the exceptional occurrence of hypercalcemia in this population. In all cases, alternative causes of hypercalcemia were ruled out, PTH was low or suppressed, and vitamin D concentrations were normal or in the range of deficiency, except in one case. Withdrawal of RANKL inhibition leads to abrupt reactivation of osteoclastogenesis, with accelerated bone resorption and a rapid influx of skeletal calcium into the bloodstream. The resulting rise in serum calcium levels appropriately suppresses PTH through physiological negative feedback mechanisms. Noteworthy, all patients had severe osteoporosis (prior fractures and/or lumbar T-score < −3), extended denosumab exposure (median 7.5 years), and markedly elevated serum CTX levels, suggesting that hypercalcemia and vertebral fractures may represent different manifestations of the same pathogenic rebound phenomenon. However, a review of the available literature highlights the few reported cases of hypercalcemia compared with the frequency of vertebral fractures following denosumab withdrawal. Thus, nearly half of the patients with hypercalcemia also presented concomitant fractures. This observation suggests that hypercalcemia may represent a clinical manifestation of the rebound increase in bone resorption after treatment discontinuation. In this context, the markedly elevated serum CTX levels, exceeding the 95th percentile of the non-juvenile age population, further support this pathophysiological mechanism [ 18 ]. Importantly, hypercalcemia in this setting was mild, asymptomatic, and resolved after the administration of antiresorptive therapy. Another relevant finding in the reported series is that none of the patients had prior exposure to bisphosphonates. Given their prolonged skeletal retention, these drugs may attenuate the rebound increase in bone resorption markers following denosumab discontinuation, thereby potentially reducing the risk of both hypercalcemia and subsequent vertebral fractures. Nevertheless, the protective effect appears to be more robust when bisphosphonate therapy is initiated immediately after denosumab withdrawal [ 19 ]. This observation reinforces the current ECTS, Endocrine Society, and Spanish Society of Bone Research and Mineral Metabolism recommendations on sequential antiresorptive therapy after denosumab discontinuation [ 4 , 5 , 17 ]. Conclusions Discontinuation of denosumab in patients with osteoporosis has been associated with a rebound increase in osteoclastic activity. Within this context, bone loss, multiple vertebral fractures, and, in rare cases, hypercalcemia may represent different clinical expressions of a similar underlying process. Hypercalcemia appears to be an uncommon and generally mild manifestation, which may share risk factors with post-discontinuation fractures. Careful monitoring and implementation of sequential antiresorptive therapy after denosumab withdrawal are essential to manage these patients and reduce the risk of vertebral fractures and disturbances of calcium metabolism.
